title: Genesis
intro: 40 days through the book of Genesis, from creation to Joseph, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: The Bible's first sentence makes its first claim: before anything else there is God, and everything that exists comes from God. In Hebrew the book is called Bereshit, "In the beginning," after its first word; Genesis means "origin." It opens the Torah, the heart of Jewish scripture, and the whole Bible for Christians. Tradition names Moses as its author; many scholars think it was woven from older sources. Starting today, 40 days through Genesis, one verse at a time.

The earth is "formless and void," dark and covered in water, when God speaks for the first time. The point is the ease of it: in Genesis, God creates by word, bringing light and order out of chaos. Light appears three days before the sun and moon. Jews and Christians read these six days in different ways: some take them literally, while others read the chapter as theological truth told through the forms of its ancient world.

The high point of the creation account. "Man" here is the Hebrew adam, meaning humankind, male and female together. Many scholars note that ancient kings were sometimes called the image of a god; Genesis gives that title to every human being. Jewish and Christian thought have long seen this verse as a foundation for human dignity.

The end of the sixth day. Through the chapter God calls what he has made "good" six times, and now, looking at the whole with humans in it, "very good," the seventh time. Jewish and Christian readers have long taken this as a basic claim about the world: the physical creation is not a mistake or a prison but something God delights in. Seven, a number of completeness, shapes the whole account; even its first verse has seven words in Hebrew.

Creation ends not with more work but with rest. God blesses the seventh day and sets it apart as holy, so the rhythm of work and rest is built into the world itself. The Hebrew verb for resting, shavat, means to stop or cease, and it is the root of Shabbat, the Sabbath. Jews keep Shabbat from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall; most Christians gather for worship on Sunday, the day of Jesus' resurrection.

Chapter 2 tells creation again, closer up and in a different style. God shapes a man from the ground like a potter and breathes life into him. Readers have long seen both sides of human nature here: made of earth, yet alive with breath from God. The Hebrew holds a pun: the man is adam, the ground is adamah. "LORD" in capitals stands for God's personal name, YHWH, which Jews traditionally don't say aloud, reading Adonai, "Lord," instead.

For the first time in Genesis, something is "not good": the man is alone. The Hebrew word for helper, ezer, is used elsewhere in the Bible mostly of God himself, so it doesn't suggest someone lesser. God then forms the woman, and the man's words on seeing her, "bone of my bones," are the first human speech recorded in the Bible.

A serpent persuades the woman to eat from the forbidden tree, the man eats too, and they hide from God among the trees. Many Jewish and Christian readers hear God's first question in the Bible as a search rather than an accusation: God seeking people out after they have gone wrong. The fruit is never named; the apple came later. Many Christians call this story "the Fall," while Jewish tradition generally reads it without the idea of inherited sin.

After God announces the consequences of their choice, the man gives his wife a name. In Hebrew she is Chavah, which sounds like the word for "living." Just after hearing that humans will return to dust, he names her for life. God then clothes them and sends them out of Eden, with cherubim guarding the way back to the tree of life.

Adam and Eve's sons: Cain farms, Abel keeps sheep. When God accepts Abel's offering but not his, Cain kills his brother in a field, the Bible's first murder. God's question gives Cain a chance to own up; instead he dodges with a question of his own. Readers have long heard the story's implied answer: yes, people are responsible for one another. Abel's Hebrew name, Hevel, means "breath" or "vapor."

Generations pass, and Genesis says violence filled the earth and God was grieved in his heart. Noah is the exception, and this short verse is the turning point: judgment is coming, but so is a fresh start through one family, saved in the ark God tells Noah to build. Older English Bibles say Noah "found grace," the word's first appearance in them. In Hebrew, the two letters of Noah's name, reversed, spell the word for favor, chen.

After the flood, God makes a covenant, a binding promise, with Noah and every living creature: never again a flood to destroy the earth. The rainbow is its sign, and the text says it is a reminder for God himself. The Hebrew word for rainbow, qeshet, is also the word for a warrior's bow, and some commentators picture God hanging up his bow in peace. Scholars have long compared the story with Mesopotamian flood tales such as Gilgamesh.

People settle in Shinar, in Mesopotamia, and build a city and a tower of baked brick. Their own words give the story its point: to reach the heavens, to "make a name" for themselves, and to avoid being scattered. Many readers see human pride and self-reliance here. God scatters them by confusing their language, and the place is called Babel, the Hebrew name for Babylon, which sounds like the Hebrew word for "confuse."

The story narrows from all humanity to one family. Abram had come with his father from Ur, in what is now southern Iraq, to Haran. Now God calls him to leave his country, his relatives and his father's household, without even saying where he is going. He sets out at 75, and that step of trust begins the story of Israel. Jews, Christians and Muslims all look to Abraham as a father of faith.

The rest of God's promise to Abram. Just before this, God says he will make Abram's name great, the very thing the builders of Babel tried to seize for themselves. Now the promise reaches past one family to "all the families of the earth." God repeats this promise to Isaac and to Jacob later in Genesis.

Abram is old and still childless, and he fears a servant will be his heir. God takes him outside under the night sky. "Credited" is a word for reckoning or counting, as if trust were entered in Abram's account. The apostle Paul later builds his teaching on faith around this verse, and Jewish tradition honors Abraham as a model of faithfulness.

Sarai, still childless, gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram, a practice known from other ancient Near Eastern texts. Mistreated by Sarai once she is pregnant, Hagar flees into the desert, where an angel tells her to name her son Ishmael, "God hears." Hagar, enslaved and a foreigner, then names God herself: El Roi, "the God who sees me." Readers have long valued the story's point that God notices those others overlook.

Thirteen years after Ishmael's birth, when Abram is 99 and Sarai still has no child, God renews the covenant. Abram, "exalted father," becomes Abraham, which the verse explains as "father of many nations." The new name is a promise he must carry long before it comes true. Sarai becomes Sarah, and circumcision is given as the covenant's sign, still marked by Jewish families on a baby boy's eighth day in the brit milah.

Three visitors arrive at Abraham's tent by the oaks of Mamre, and he rushes to feed them. When one says Sarah will have a son, she laughs to herself, since she is about 90. This question is the reply, and the heart of the story: nothing God promises is beyond God's power. Jewish tradition generally sees the visitors as angels, while Andrei Rublev's famous Russian icon reads them as an image of the Christian Trinity.

God reveals that he is about to judge the wicked cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, and Abraham pushes back. He bargains like a trader: would God spare the city for 50 righteous people? For 45? He talks God down to ten. It is one of the Bible's boldest moments, a human being arguing with God for the sake of justice.

After 25 years of waiting since the first promise, Sarah gives birth to a son, and Abraham is 100. Abraham names him Isaac, in Hebrew Yitzchak, which means "he laughs." The laughter that once came from disbelief turns into laughter of joy, shared with everyone who hears the news.

One of the hardest stories in the Bible. God tests Abraham by telling him to offer Isaac as a sacrifice, and on the way up the mountain Isaac asks where the lamb is. Abraham's answer is a statement of trust, and it comes true: an angel stops him, and a ram is offered instead. In Judaism the story is the Akedah, "the binding," read in synagogues at Rosh Hashanah. Many Christians see it as foreshadowing Jesus, the "Lamb of God."

posts.display: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you will be separated; one people will be stronger than the other, and the older will serve the younger.”
posts.caption: Isaac marries Rebekah, and after twenty years she becomes pregnant with twins who struggle inside her. When she asks God why, this is the answer: her sons will become two rival nations, Israel and Edom, and the usual order will be reversed. The second twin is born gripping his brother's heel, so he is named Jacob, from the Hebrew word for heel. Again and again, Genesis favors a younger son over an older one.

Esau had already traded his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of stew. Now Isaac is old and nearly blind, and Rebekah helps Jacob disguise himself as Esau, with goatskins on his hands and neck, to take his father's blessing. Isaac is suspicious but blesses him anyway. Genesis doesn't hide the deceit: the chosen family is deeply flawed, and Jacob will spend years living with the consequences.

Fleeing his brother's anger, Jacob stops for the night with a stone for a pillow. He dreams of a ladder, or perhaps a stairway, joining earth and heaven, and at the top God repeats the promise once given to Abraham. Many readers see the point in who receives it: a runaway who has just deceived his family finds that heaven is not out of reach. "Jacob's ladder" became the subject of a well-known African American spiritual.

Jacob wakes from his dream amazed. He had thought he was just stopping at "a certain place," and finds God was there all along. Many readers take this as the point of the scene: God's presence can be found in unlikely, ordinary places. Jacob sets up his stone pillow as a pillar, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel, "house of God," later an important center of worship in ancient Israel.

Jacob reaches his mother's family and falls in love with his cousin Rachel at a well. He agrees to work seven years for her father, Laban, and love makes the years feel like days. But on the wedding night Laban swaps in Rachel's older sister, Leah, and Jacob, who once deceived his own father, is deceived in turn. He works seven more years for Rachel.

Twenty years later, Jacob heads home to face Esau, who is coming with 400 men. The night before, alone by the Jabbok River, he wrestles a mysterious man until dawn and won't let go, even with a wounded hip. Many readers see Jacob's whole life here: he has always grabbed for blessing, and now he clings to God for it. The prophet Hosea calls the man an angel; Jacob names the place Peniel, "face of God."

After wrestling all night, Jacob gets a new name. His old name recalled grabbing a heel, and its sound, cheating; the new one, Israel, the verse explains as one who has "struggled with God." Many readers find it striking that a whole people is named for wrestling with God. The name passes to his twelve sons, ancestors of Israel's twelve tribes. Jacob leaves limping, and Jewish dietary law still avoids the hip tendon of animals because of this story.

Twenty years after Jacob cheated him, Esau comes to meet him with 400 men, and Jacob approaches bowing to the ground seven times, expecting the worst. Instead Esau runs to him and embraces him, and the two brothers weep together. The wronged brother is the one who runs to embrace the guilty one. Many readers hear an echo of this scene in Jesus' parable of the prodigal son, where a father runs to embrace his returning son.

The last part of Genesis follows Joseph, son of Jacob, who is called Israel here. His father's open favoritism, and the special robe that shows it, start the trouble: along with Joseph's dreams of his family bowing to him, they turn his brothers' jealousy into hatred. The Hebrew words for the robe are uncertain, possibly a long robe with sleeves; "many colors" comes from the ancient Greek translation, and later inspired the musical Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat.

Joseph's brothers sell him to traders for twenty pieces of silver, and he becomes a slave in the house of Potiphar, an Egyptian officer. "The LORD was with Joseph" echoes through this chapter, even after Potiphar's wife falsely accuses him and he lands in prison. God never speaks to Joseph directly; instead the story shows God quietly at work behind the scenes.

Two years after Joseph explains a fellow prisoner's dream, Pharaoh has dreams no one can interpret: seven thin cows devouring seven fat ones. Joseph is brought out of the dungeon, gives the credit to God, and explains: seven years of plenty, then seven of famine. Pharaoh puts him over all Egypt at age 30, thirteen years after his brothers sold him.

The famine reaches Canaan, and Jacob sends ten of his sons to Egypt to buy grain. They bow before the governor, not realizing he is the brother they sold, now an Egyptian official speaking through an interpreter. Joseph's boyhood dream of his brothers' sheaves bowing to his has come true.

Joseph tests his brothers by planting his silver cup in the sack of Benjamin, the youngest, and threatening to keep him as a slave. Judah, who once proposed selling Joseph, now offers to stay as a slave in Benjamin's place, ending his plea with these words about their father. The point is how much he has changed: the brother who sold a brother now gives himself up for one. The word "Jew" comes from Judah's name.

Judah's plea breaks Joseph. He sends his servants out and weeps so loudly that the Egyptians hear him. Then he tells his terrified brothers who he is, and goes further: God, he says, sent him ahead of them to save lives.

Joseph sends wagons to bring his father Jacob, also called Israel, and the whole family to Egypt, and God tells Jacob in a vision not to be afraid to go. Jacob had believed for over twenty years that Joseph was dead. Father and son meet in the land of Goshen, and Joseph embraces him and weeps for a long time.

Joseph presents his father to Pharaoh, and it is the old shepherd who blesses the king. Asked his age, Jacob answers with striking honesty: he calls his life a journey, a stay in places not his own, and its years few and hard. At 130, that is short by his family's measure: Abraham lived to 175 and Isaac to 180. Jacob's own years had included exile, deception and long grief.

Jacob's long, troubled life ends quietly. On his deathbed he has spoken a poem over each of his twelve sons, including a promise of the scepter to Judah, a line ancient Jewish interpreters and Christians alike read as pointing to the Messiah. He asks to be buried in the cave of Machpelah with Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah. "Gathered to his people" is a Hebrew way of describing death as rejoining those who went before.

After Jacob dies, Joseph's brothers fear he has only been waiting to take revenge. Instead he forgives them, and this line sums up the whole Joseph story. Genesis ends with the family settled in Egypt, setting the stage for the book of Exodus. That's the whole of Genesis. Thank you for reading it with me.
